title: Out of Bounds Definition
body: Out of bounds is the area outside the defined boundaries of the course, marked by white stakes or lines. When ball is OB, the entire ball must be outside the boundary to be OB. Stakes themselves are OB. If boundary line is used, the line itself is OB. A ball on the line is out of bounds.

title: Out of Bounds Penalty
body: When your ball is out of bounds, you must take stroke-and-distance relief: add one penalty stroke and play again from where you last played. This is the most severe penalty in golf. From the tee, you're now hitting 3. From fairway, count your strokes and add one, then replay from same spot.

title: Provisional Ball Purpose
body: A provisional ball is played when your original ball may be lost outside a penalty area or may be out of bounds. The provisional saves time—you don't have to return to the original spot if you can't find your ball. Announce 'I'm playing a provisional' before hitting it.

title: Provisional Ball Procedure
body: To play a provisional: announce your intention clearly before playing, play from the same place as the original. Continue playing the provisional until you reach the area where the original is likely to be. If original is found in bounds, pick up the provisional. If original is lost/OB, the provisional becomes ball in play.

title: Lost Ball Definition
body: A ball is lost if not found within 3 minutes of the player or caddie beginning to search for it. The 3-minute search time begins when you reach the area and start looking. If not found in time, return to where you played the previous stroke and play under stroke and distance.

title: Penalty Area Definition
body: A penalty area is an area from which relief with a one-stroke penalty is allowed. Marked by yellow stakes/lines or red stakes/lines. The ball is in a penalty area when any part of it lies in or touches the area. Stakes are inside the penalty area. You may play from a penalty area without penalty.

title: Yellow Penalty Area Relief
body: Yellow penalty area (typically crosses line of play): with one-stroke penalty, options are: 1) Stroke-and-distance—replay from previous spot. 2) Back-on-line relief—drop on a line from the hole through where ball last crossed the edge, going back as far as desired. You may also play the ball as it lies without penalty.

title: Red Penalty Area Relief
body: Red penalty area (typically runs alongside play): includes all yellow penalty area options plus lateral relief—drop within two club-lengths of where ball last crossed the edge, no nearer the hole, or within two club-lengths of a point on opposite edge equidistant from hole. One-stroke penalty for relief options.

title: Unplayable Ball Declaration
body: You may declare your ball unplayable anywhere on the course except in a penalty area. No need to justify the decision—you simply decide. This costs one penalty stroke. You have three relief options to choose from after declaring unplayable. It's often the best choice when attempting the shot would likely make things worse.

title: Unplayable Ball Relief Options
body: After declaring unplayable (one-stroke penalty), options are: 1) Stroke-and-distance—return to previous spot. 2) Back-on-line—drop on line from hole through ball position, going back as far as desired. 3) Lateral—drop within two club-lengths of ball position, no nearer hole. In bunker, options 2 and 3 must stay in bunker unless you take two-stroke penalty to drop outside.

title: Proper Dropping Procedure
body: When taking relief, you must drop the ball correctly: stand outside the relief area, hold the ball at knee height, drop it straight down. The ball must come to rest in the relief area. If it rolls out, re-drop. If it rolls out again, place it where it first touched ground on the second drop.

title: Relief Area Definition
body: Relief area is where the ball must be dropped and come to rest when taking relief. Size varies by rule: one club-length for most free relief, two club-lengths for lateral unplayable and red penalty area lateral relief. Measure with longest club in bag except putter. Ball must be dropped in and stay in the relief area.

title: Cart Path Relief
body: Cart paths are immovable obstructions. Free relief when path interferes with lie, stance, or swing. Find nearest point of complete relief no nearer hole, then drop within one club-length. You cannot choose which side to drop—must use nearest point. You may decline relief and play from the path if you prefer.

title: Nearest Point of Complete Relief
body: The nearest point of complete relief is the reference point for free relief situations. It's the nearest point where the condition no longer interferes with stance, swing, and lie—and no nearer the hole. Use the club you would have used for the stroke. Mark this point, then measure your relief area from it.

title: Ground Under Repair
body: Ground under repair (GUR) is area marked by course as being repaired or damaged. Marked by white lines or blue stakes, or may be declared by official. Free relief available if GUR interferes with lie, stance, or swing. Find nearest point of complete relief outside GUR, no nearer hole, drop within one club-length.

title: Temporary Water Relief
body: Temporary water (casual water) is any accumulation of water visible before or after taking stance that isn't in a penalty area. Free relief when it interferes with lie, stance, or swing. Find nearest point of complete relief where water doesn't affect you, no nearer hole, drop within one club-length.

title: Embedded Ball Relief
body: Free relief for embedded ball in the general area (not bunkers or penalty areas). Ball must be embedded in its own pitch-mark. Procedure: mark position, lift ball, clean it, drop within one club-length of where ball was embedded, no nearer hole. Ball must be embedded—sitting down in soft ground doesn't qualify.

title: Bunker Basic Rules
body: In bunkers, you may not touch sand with your club before making a stroke when ball is in bunker (testing condition). You may remove loose impediments. If ball moves while removing impediment: replace ball with one-stroke penalty. You may touch sand when entering bunker, during backswing, or in making a practice swing not in the sand near the ball.

title: Unplayable in Bunker
body: If you declare ball unplayable in a bunker, the back-on-line and lateral relief options must result in dropping in the bunker (one-stroke penalty). For an additional penalty stroke (two total), you may drop outside the bunker on the back-on-line. Stroke-and-distance always takes you to where you played from.

title: Putting Green Rules Overview
body: On the putting green you may: mark, lift, and clean your ball; repair pitch-marks and old hole plugs; remove loose impediments and movable obstructions. You may not repair spike marks or other damage not caused by ball impact. The flagstick may be left in or removed—no penalty if ball strikes attended or unattended flagstick.

title: Marking Your Ball
body: To mark ball on green: place ball-marker immediately behind or beside the ball, then lift. To replace: set ball in front of marker, then remove marker. If ball-marker interferes with another player, move it one or more clubhead-lengths to the side, then remember to replace it before playing. Use a flat object that won't roll.

title: Ball Moved on Putting Green
body: If ball on putting green is accidentally moved by you, your partner, or your equipment: no penalty, replace the ball. If moved by wind, water, or other natural force after you've marked and replaced it: replace. If moved by natural forces before you've marked it: play from new position. This protects players from random movements.

title: Flagstick Rules
body: You may leave flagstick in hole, have it removed, or have it attended. If attended, it must be removed after stroke is made. If ball strikes flagstick (in or out of hole), there's no penalty. You may not have flagstick moved to influence ball's movement while ball is in motion. Personal preference—studies suggest leaving in helps.

title: Playing Wrong Ball
body: Playing a wrong ball in stroke play: two-stroke penalty. Strokes made with wrong ball don't count. You must correct the mistake by playing the correct ball. In match play: loss of hole. To avoid: clearly mark your ball, check before each stroke. Exception: no penalty for wrong ball played from penalty area if corrected.

title: Loose Impediments
body: Loose impediments are natural objects not fixed or growing: leaves, stones, twigs, branches, dead animals, worms, insects. You may remove them anywhere on course without penalty, including bunkers. If ball moves while removing in general area or green: replace without penalty. If ball moves while removing in bunker: one-stroke penalty, replace ball.

title: Movable Obstructions
body: Movable obstructions are artificial objects that can be reasonably moved: rakes, bottles, cans, flagstick when removed, etc. You may move them without penalty. If ball moves during removal: replace without penalty. If ball is in or on the obstruction: lift ball, move obstruction, drop ball where it was (or place on green).

title: Immovable Obstructions
body: Immovable obstructions are artificial objects that cannot be easily moved: buildings, cart paths, permanent fixtures, sprinkler heads. Free relief when obstruction interferes with lie, stance, or swing (not line of play, except on green). Find nearest point of complete relief, drop within one club-length. You may decline and play as it lies.

title: Order of Play
body: Traditionally, player farthest from hole plays first. On tee, player with best score on previous hole has honor. Ready golf is encouraged in stroke play—player who is ready may play if safe. In match play, playing out of turn allows opponent to recall the stroke. Be aware of safety; don't hit if others are in range.

title: Ready Golf
body: Ready golf means playing when ready rather than strict order, encouraged to speed pace of play. Hit when safe and ready, even if not farthest from hole. Don't wait for others to finish pre-shot routines. Putt out if convenient. Search briefly, then let others play while you look. Safety first, but don't waste time.

title: Pace of Play
body: Players should maintain pace of play and keep up with group ahead. Target: 4 hours for 18 holes. Tips: be ready when it's your turn, limit practice swings, search max 3 minutes, walk briskly between shots. If you fall behind, take steps to catch up. Let faster groups through if you're holding up play.

title: Maximum 14 Clubs
body: You may carry a maximum of 14 clubs during a round. Penalty for more: two strokes per hole played with excess clubs (maximum four strokes in stroke play). In match play: deduct one hole for each hole excess was carried (maximum two holes). You may start with fewer than 14 and add during round if you don't delay play.

title: Ball Moved During Search
body: If you accidentally move your ball while searching for it: no penalty. Replace the ball in its original position (estimate if exact spot is unknown). If ball was covered by loose impediments or sand, only re-cover enough to see a small part of ball. This prevents penalty for unfortunate accidents during legitimate search.

title: Practice Strokes During Round
body: During a round, you may not make a practice stroke at any ball on the course. You may make practice swings anywhere. Between holes, you may practice putting on the green just completed, any practice green, and the next teeing area. You may not unreasonably delay play to practice. Practice strokes differ from practice swings.

title: Advice Rules
body: You may not give or ask for advice during a round, except from your partner or caddie. Advice is any suggestion that could influence decisions about play, club selection, or how to make a stroke. You may ask anyone about rules, distances, or positions of hazards (public information). Penalty: two strokes or loss of hole.

title: Improving Lie or Conditions
body: You may not improve your lie, area of intended stance, area of intended swing, or line of play by: moving, bending, or breaking anything growing or fixed; creating or eliminating irregularities; removing or pressing down sand, soil, or grass; removing dew, frost, or water. Exception: fairly taking your stance and making a normal swing.

title: Play Ball as It Lies
body: The fundamental principle: play the ball as it lies and the course as you find it. Don't move the ball to improve position. Don't modify surroundings to improve shot. Exceptions are specific (relief situations). This tests your ability to handle whatever conditions arise. Honest adherence is the foundation of golf integrity.

title: Identifying Your Ball
body: You're responsible for playing the correct ball. To identify: you may mark and lift the ball. Announce your intention; give opponent/marker chance to observe. Mark the spot, lift only enough to identify. Don't clean more than necessary. If it's yours, replace it. If not yours, ball is lost. Call a penalty on yourself if needed.

title: Ball in Motion
body: You may not deliberately deflect or stop a ball in motion. If your ball in motion is accidentally deflected by you, your equipment, or your caddie: no penalty in most cases, play ball as it lies. If deliberately deflected: general penalty and ball is played as it lies. Exception: ball stopped on flagstick or equipment may be placed at estimated spot.

title: Scorecard Responsibility
body: In stroke play, you're responsible for the accuracy of hole-by-hole scores on your card. Sign your card to certify scores. If you record a score lower than actually taken: disqualification. If higher than taken: that higher score stands. The Committee totals the scores. Verify carefully before signing.

title: Double Hit
body: If you accidentally hit the ball twice in one stroke (double hit): no penalty, count it as one stroke. Play the ball as it lies. This rule changed in 2019—previously each contact was a separate stroke. Now all contacts in a single stroke intention count as one stroke, regardless of how many times you contacted the ball.

title: Wrong Putting Green
body: If your ball is on a wrong putting green (green for a different hole), you must take free relief. You may not play from a wrong green. Find nearest point of complete relief off the green, not nearer hole, and drop within one club-length. This protects the putting surfaces from unnecessary traffic.

title: Animal Hole Relief
body: Free relief is available from animal holes, animal droppings, and animal paths in the general area if they interfere with lie, stance, or swing. Animal holes include holes made by any animal except worms or insects. Find nearest point of complete relief, drop within one club-length, no nearer hole.

title: When Ball Is Holed
body: A ball is holed when it lies at rest within the circumference of the hole and all of it is below the level of the lip of the hole. If ball is leaning against flagstick and part is below lip: remove flagstick—if ball falls in, it's holed; if it moves away from hole, place it on lip.

title: Teeing Area Rules
body: Teeing area is where you start each hole, defined by two tee markers and extending two club-lengths back. Ball must be teed within this area but you may stand outside it. If ball falls off tee before stroke: re-tee without penalty. You may use a tee, mound of sand, or place ball on ground.

title: Playing from Outside Teeing Area
body: If you play from outside the teeing area in stroke play: two-stroke penalty and must correct by playing from within teeing area before starting next hole. The stroke from outside doesn't count. In match play: opponent may cancel the stroke and require you to replay from correct area. Watch for accidentally teeing ahead of markers.

title: Repairing Pitch Marks
body: You may repair pitch marks (ball marks) and old hole plugs on the putting green anytime, whether or not your ball is on the green. Use a repair tool: push edges toward center without lifting core. Do not repair spike marks or other damage not caused by ball impact. Repair at least one extra mark beyond your own.

title: Divot Etiquette
body: While not a rule with penalties, replacing divots or filling with sand/seed mix is expected etiquette. In fairway, replace the divot piece or fill with provided mixture. On driving range, follow the facility's divot pattern. A ball in a divot must be played as it lies—no free relief. Proper divot care maintains course condition.

title: Bunker Etiquette
body: After playing from a bunker, rake your footprints and the area you disturbed. Enter from low side nearest your ball to minimize disturbance. Rake toward center, smoothing sand. Replace rake as course directs. Leaving bunker unraked for next player is poor etiquette. Take time to leave bunker as you'd want to find it.

title: General Penalty Definition
body: The general penalty is two strokes in stroke play or loss of hole in match play. This applies to most rule violations unless a specific penalty is stated. Examples: playing wrong ball, improving lie, giving/asking advice. When rules refer to 'general penalty,' this is what applies.

title: Playing from Penalty Areas
body: You may always play your ball from a penalty area without penalty. Before stroke: you may remove loose impediments, touch or move ground with club. You may not test the condition of the water. After playing: if ball stays in penalty area, you may play again or take relief. You only add penalty strokes if you take relief.

title: What Counts as a Stroke
body: A stroke is the forward movement of the club made to strike the ball. If you start the downswing with intent to hit the ball, it counts as a stroke even if you miss completely. Stopping the downswing before impact is not a stroke. Practice swings are not strokes because there's no intent to hit the ball.

title: Interference Meaning
body: Interference exists when a condition physically affects: your ball, your area of intended stance, your area of intended swing, or (on putting green) your line of play. It's not interference if the condition is merely in your field of vision. The condition must actually affect how you would play the shot.

title: Measuring Club-Lengths
body: When rules require measuring club-lengths (for relief areas), use the longest club in your bag except the putter—usually your driver. The club-length is measured from the grip end to the toe. Always use the same club for consistency. You cannot change clubs mid-measurement or use putter for a longer shaft.

title: Local Rules Overview
body: Local rules modify or supplement the main rules for specific course conditions. Found on scorecard or posted in clubhouse. Common local rules: preferred lies (lift-clean-place), out of bounds lines, environmental areas, distance measuring devices allowed. Always check local rules before playing—they affect how you handle certain situations.

title: Preferred Lies (Winter Rules)
body: Preferred lies is a local rule allowing ball improvement in fairway during poor conditions. When in effect: mark ball in fairway, lift, clean, place within specified distance (usually 6 inches or one club-length), no nearer hole. Does not apply in rough. Check if in effect before using—it's not always allowed.

title: Handicap Posting Basics
body: Post scores from all rounds of at least 9 holes played under Rules of Golf. Include penalty scores and incomplete rounds (use expected score for unfinished holes). Don't cherry-pick good rounds only. Post promptly after round. Accurate posting creates fair handicap. The system uses best 8 of last 20 differentials.

title: Net Double Bogey Maximum
body: When posting scores for handicap, you cannot take more than net double bogey on any hole. Net double bogey = par + 2 + any handicap strokes you receive on that hole. Example: on a par 4 where you get 1 stroke, maximum score to post is 7 (4+2+1). This prevents blow-up holes from distorting handicap.

title: Match Play Basics
body: In match play, you play against an opponent, not the course. Each hole is a separate contest. Winner of hole gets 'up'; tied hole is halved. Match won when one player is up by more holes than remain. You may concede a stroke, hole, or match anytime. Play out of turn may be recalled by opponent.

title: Stroke Play Basics
body: In stroke play, you compete against the entire field by total strokes. Every stroke counts. The player with lowest total wins. You must complete every hole—can't pick up without penalty. If you fail to hole out and don't correct before starting next hole: disqualification. Stroke play is the most common format.

title: Stableford Scoring
body: Stableford awards points based on score relative to par: double bogey or worse = 0, bogey = 1, par = 2, birdie = 3, eagle = 4, albatross = 5. Highest point total wins. Advantage: one bad hole doesn't ruin round—just pick up and take 0 points. Good format for casual play and improving golfers.

title: Concession in Match Play
body: In match play, you may concede opponent's next stroke, hole, or match at any time before outcome is decided. A concession cannot be declined or withdrawn. Common to concede short putts for pace. Strategy: don't concede anything you want to see them attempt. Once conceded, the putt/hole/match is considered made/won.

title: Honor on Teeing Ground
body: The player with lowest score on previous hole has honor (plays first) on next tee. On first hole, order is determined by draw, ballot, or agreement. In fourball or foursomes, team honor applies. With ready golf, strict honor is often relaxed—whoever's ready may play first if safe. Honor is about respect and tradition.

title: Golf Courtesy Basics
body: Core courtesies: stay still and quiet while others play; don't stand in their line of sight; keep pace; replace divots and repair pitch marks; rake bunkers; let faster groups through. Golf is self-policed—courtesy enables enjoyable play for everyone. Treat others as you'd want to be treated. Respect the game's traditions.
